column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 23: “Purification is half of faith”

column2: From Abū Mālik al-Ashʿarī (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Purification is half of faith. Al-ḥamdu lillāh (praise be to Allah) fills the Scale. Subḥān Allāh (glory be to Allah) and al-ḥamdu lillāh

fill — or: fills — what is between the heavens and the earth. Prayer is light, charity is a proof, and patience is radiance. The Qurʾān is a proof for you or against you. Everyone goes out in the morning and sells himself, either freeing himself or ruining himself.” Muslim reported it.
Muslim recorded this hadith through the narration of Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr: Zayd ibn Sallām told him that Abū Sallām told him, from Abū Mālik al-Ashʿarī,
who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Purification is half of faith, and al-ḥamdu lillāh fills the Scale” — and he mentioned the hadith.
In most copies of Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim it reads “and patience is radiance”, and in some, “and fasting is radiance”.

There is disagreement about whether Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr heard from Zayd ibn Sallām: Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn denied it and Imam Aḥmad affirmed it. In this narration he states explicitly that he heard it from him.

Al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah recorded this hadith through the narration of Muʿāwiyah ibn Sallām, from his brother Zayd ibn Sallām, from his grandfather Abū Sallām, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ghanm, from Abū Mālik, thus adding ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ghanm to its chain.
Some of the ḥāfiẓ scholars preferred this narration, saying: Muʿāwiyah ibn Sallām knew his brother Zayd's hadith better than Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr did.
This is strengthened by its having been narrated from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ghanm, from Abū Mālik, by another route. In that case Muslim's narration would be broken (munqaṭiʿ).
Muʿāwiyah's narration differs somewhat from that of Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr; its wording in Ibn Mājah is: “Performing wuḍūʾ thoroughly is half of faith; al-ḥamdu lillāh is the fill of the Scale;

tasbīḥ [saying subḥān Allāh] and takbīr [saying Allāhu akbar] are the fill of heaven and earth; prayer is light, zakāh is a proof, patience is radiance, and the Qurʾān is a proof for you or against you. Everyone goes out in the morning and sells himself, either freeing himself or ruining himself.”
Al-Tirmidhī recorded the hadith of Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr that Muslim recorded, in the wording:
“Wuḍūʾ is half of faith,” the rest of his hadith following Muslim's text.
Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of a man of Banū Sulaym, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ counted them out on my hand — or on his own hand:
“Tasbīḥ is half the Scale, al-ḥamdu lillāh fills it, takbīr fills what is between heaven and earth, fasting is half of patience, and purification is half of faith.”

As for his words ﷺ, “Purification is half of faith”: some explained purification here as leaving sins, as in the words of the Exalted, “They are people who keep themselves pure” [al-Aʿrāf 7:82], “And purify your garments” [al-Muddaththir 74:4], and “Indeed, Allah loves those who repent and loves those who purify themselves” [al-Baqarah 2:222].

He said: Faith is of two kinds, doing and leaving: half of it is doing what is commanded, and half of it is leaving what is forbidden, which is purifying the soul by leaving sins. This view would be possible, were it not that the narration
“Wuḍūʾ is half of faith” rules it out, as does the narration “Performing wuḍūʾ thoroughly”.

It is also questionable in terms of meaning, for many deeds purify the soul of past sins, such as prayer; how, then, could they not come under the name “purification”? And once deeds, or some of them, come under the name “purification”, it no longer holds that leaving sins is half of faith.

The correct view, held by most, is that purification here means purifying oneself with water from ritual impurity. That is why Muslim recorded it at the opening of the chapters on wuḍūʾ, and al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Mājah and others recorded it likewise. On this basis, people have differed over what it means for purification with water to be half of faith.
Some said that “half” (shaṭr) here means a part, not exactly half, so that purification is a part of faith. This is weak,
because in the language shaṭr is known to be used only for a half,
and because in the hadith of the man of Banū Sulaym it is “Purification is half (niṣf) of faith,” as mentioned above.
Some said: The meaning is that the reward of wuḍūʾ is multiplied until it reaches half the reward of faith — faith's reward, that is, without multiplication. This is questionable and far-fetched.

Some said: Faith expiates all the major sins, and wuḍūʾ expiates the minor ones, so in this respect it is half of faith. This is refuted by the hadith “Whoever does evil in Islam will be taken to account for what he did in the Jāhiliyyah,” which has been mentioned earlier.
Some said: Wuḍūʾ expiates sins together with faith, and so it has become half of faith. This is weak.

Some said: Faith here means prayer, as in the words of the Mighty and Majestic, “And Allah would never let your faith go to waste” [al-Baqarah 2:143], meaning your prayer towards Bayt al-Maqdis. If faith means prayer, then, since prayer is accepted only with purification, purification is in this respect half of prayer.
Muḥammad ibn Naṣr al-Marwazī related this interpretation in Kitāb al-Ṣalāh from Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh, from Yaḥyā ibn Ādam,
adding that Yaḥyā said, concerning the meaning of the saying “‘I do not know’ is half of knowledge”: Knowledge consists only of “I know” and “I do not know”, so each is one half of it.
I say: Whatever has two kinds under it, each of them is a half of it, whether the two kinds are equal in number or one is greater than the other. This is shown by the hadith,

“I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves.” What is meant is the recitation in the prayer, which is why He explained it with al-Fātiḥah; and what is meant is that it is divided between worship and asking — worship being the Lord's right and asking the servant's right — not that its words are divided equally.

Al-Khaṭṭābī mentioned this, citing as evidence the Arabs' saying, “Half the year is travel and half of it is staying at home” — which, he said, does not mean that the two periods are equal, but that time is divided between them, even if their lengths differ. He also cited the words of Shurayḥ, when he was asked: How are you this morning?

He said: I am this morning with half the people angry with me — meaning that people are either those for whom judgement is given or those against whom it is given; the one judged against is angry, and the one judged for is pleased with him; so they are two different parties. And the poet says:
When I die, people will be in two halves: one gloating / over my death, the other praising what I used to do.
He means that they will be divided into two groups.

I say: Of this meaning is the hadith of Abū Hurayrah traced back to the Prophet ﷺ (marfūʿ) about the fixed shares of inheritance (farāʾiḍ), “They are half of knowledge,” recorded by Ibn Mājah. For the rulings that apply to those who are morally responsible are of two kinds: one relates to life, and one to what comes after death, which is the farāʾiḍ.
Ibn Masʿūd said: The farāʾiḍ are a third of knowledge.

The basis for that is the hadith recorded by Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah from the hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, as marfūʿ: “Knowledge is three, and whatever is besides that is extra: a decisive verse, an established sunnah, or a just obligation (farīḍah).”

It is narrated that Mujāhid said: Rinsing the mouth and the nose is half of wuḍūʾ. Perhaps he meant that wuḍūʾ has two parts, one mentioned in the Qurʾān and the other taken from the Sunnah, namely rinsing the mouth and nose;

or he meant that rinsing the mouth and nose purifies the inside of the body, while washing the other limbs purifies its outside, so that in this respect they are two halves. Of this kind is Ibn Masʿūd's saying: Patience is half of faith, and certainty is the whole of faith.
It has come through the narration of Yazīd al-Raqāshī from Anas, as marfūʿ: “Faith is two halves: half in patience and half in gratitude.” Since faith includes doing the obligations
and leaving what is forbidden, and none of that is attained except by patience, patience is half of faith. In the same way it is said of wuḍūʾ that it is half of prayer.
Moreover, prayer expiates sins and wrongdoings on condition that wuḍūʾ is done thoroughly and well, so in this respect too wuḍūʾ is half of prayer, as in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim from ʿUthmān,

that the Prophet ﷺ said: “There is no Muslim who purifies himself, completing the purification prescribed for him, and then prays these five prayers, but they are an expiation for what is between them.”
In another narration of his: “Whoever completes wuḍūʾ as Allah has commanded him, the obligatory prayers are expiations for what is between them.”
Moreover, prayer is the key to Paradise and wuḍūʾ is the key to prayer, as Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī recorded from the hadith of Jābir, as marfūʿ.

Both prayer and wuḍūʾ bring about the opening of the gates of Paradise, as in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim from ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir, who heard the Prophet ﷺ say: “There is no Muslim who performs wuḍūʾ and does it well, then stands and prays two rakʿahs,
attending to them with his heart and his face, but Paradise becomes his due.” And from ʿUqbah, from ʿUmar, the Prophet ﷺ said: “There is none of you who performs wuḍūʾ completely — or thoroughly —

and then says, ‘I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muḥammad is His servant and Messenger,’ but the eight gates of Paradise are opened for him, and he may enter by whichever he wishes.”
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from ʿUbādah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever says, ‘I bear witness that there is no god but Allah alone, without partner, and that Muḥammad is His servant and Messenger,

and that ʿĪsā is the servant of Allah, the son of His maidservant, His word which He cast to Maryam and a spirit from Him, and that Paradise is true and the Fire is true,’ Allah will admit him by whichever of the eight gates of Paradise he wishes.”
So if wuḍūʾ together with the two testimonies brings about the opening of the gates of Paradise, wuḍūʾ is in this respect half of faith in Allah and His Messenger.
Moreover, wuḍūʾ is one of the hidden qualities of faith that none keeps up except a believer, as in the hadith of Thawbān and others from the Prophet ﷺ: “None guards his wuḍūʾ except a believer.”
It has also been reported that washing after major ritual impurity (janābah) is the fulfilment of a trust, as al-ʿUqaylī recorded from the hadith of Abū al-Dardāʾ, that the Prophet ﷺ said:
“There are five things: whoever brings them together with faith will enter Paradise. Whoever keeps up the five prayers, with their wuḍūʾ, their bowing, their prostrations and their times;

gives the zakāh from his wealth willingly” — the narrator said: and he used to say, “By Allah, none does that but a believer” — “fasts Ramaḍān, makes pilgrimage to the House if he is able to find a way to it, and fulfils the trust.” They said: Abū al-Dardāʾ, what is fulfilling the trust?
He said: Washing after janābah, for Allah has not entrusted the son of Ādam with anything of his religion other than it.

Ibn Mājah recorded, from the hadith of Abū Ayyūb, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The five prayers, and from one Friday to the next, and fulfilling the trust, are an expiation for what is between them.” He was asked: What is fulfilling the trust?
He said: “Washing after janābah, for under every hair there is janābah.” The hadith of Abū al-Dardāʾ before it makes wuḍūʾ one of the parts of prayer.

It has come in another hadith, recorded by al-Bazzār through the narration of Shabābah ibn Sawwār: al-Mughīrah ibn Muslim told us, from al-Aʿmash, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Abū Hurayrah, as marfūʿ: “Prayer is three thirds: purification is a third, bowing is a third,

and prostration is a third. Whoever performs it as it should be performed, it is accepted from him and the rest of his deeds are accepted from him; and whoever has his prayer rejected has the rest of his deeds rejected.” He said: Al-Mughīrah alone narrated it; the well-preserved version is from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Kaʿb, as his own words.
On this division wuḍūʾ is a third of prayer — unless bowing and prostration are treated as one thing because they are similar in form, in which case wuḍūʾ is again half of prayer.
It might also be said that all the qualities of faith, deeds and words alike, purify and cleanse the heart, whereas purification with water is particular to purifying and cleaning the body.

So the qualities of faith are of two kinds, one purifying the outward and the other the inward, and in this respect they are two halves. And Allah knows best what He and His Messenger meant in all of this.

As for his words ﷺ, “Al-ḥamdu lillāh fills the Scale, and subḥān Allāh and al-ḥamdu lillāh fill — or: fills — what is between the heavens and the earth”: this is the narrator's doubt about the wording. In the narration of al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah: “Tasbīḥ and takbīr are the fill of heaven and earth.”
In the hadith of the man of Banū Sulaym: “Tasbīḥ is half the Scale, al-ḥamdu lillāh fills it, and takbīr fills what is between heaven and earth.”
Al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of al-Ifrīqī, from ʿAbdullāh ibn Yazīd, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, that the Prophet ﷺ said:
“Tasbīḥ is half the Scale, al-ḥamdu lillāh fills it, and lā ilāha illā Allāh has no veil before Allah until it reaches Him.” He said: Its chain is not strong.

I say: There is disagreement over its chain from al-Ifrīqī; it has been narrated from him, from Abū ʿAlqamah, from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, with an addition: “And Allāhu akbar is the fill of the heavens and the earth.”

Jaʿfar al-Firyābī narrated in Kitāb al-Dhikr, as did others, from the hadith of ʿAlī, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Al-ḥamdu lillāh is the fill of the Scale, subḥān Allāh is half the Scale, and lā ilāha illā Allāh and Allāhu akbar are the fill of the heavens and the earth and what is between them.”

Al-Firyābī also recorded, from the hadith of Muʿādh ibn Jabal, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “There are two phrases: one of them, when someone says it, has nothing to hold it back short of the Throne, and the other fills what is between heaven and earth: lā ilāha illā Allāh and Allāhu akbar.”
These hadiths, then, set out the merit of these four phrases, which are the best of speech: subḥān Allāh, al-ḥamdu lillāh, lā ilāha illā Allāh and Allāhu akbar.
As for al-ḥamdu lillāh, the hadiths all agree that it fills the Scale. It has been said that this is a parable, meaning that if praise were a body it would fill the Scale. It has also been said

that, rather, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will give the deeds and words of the children of Ādam forms that will be seen and weighed on the Day of Resurrection, as the Prophet ﷺ said: “The Qurʾān will come on the Day of Resurrection, led by al-Baqarah and Āl ʿImrān, as though they were two clouds, or two canopies, or two flocks of birds in rows.”
And he said: “Two phrases beloved to the Most Merciful, heavy in the Scale, light on the tongue: subḥān Allāh wa-bi-ḥamdihi, subḥān Allāh al-ʿAẓīm.”

And he said: “The heaviest thing placed in the Scale is good character.” Likewise, the believer's righteous deeds come to him in his grave in the finest form, and the disbeliever's deeds come to him in the ugliest form.
It is narrated that prayer, zakāh, fasting and deeds of righteousness will be around the dead person in his grave, defending him, and that the Qurʾān will ascend and intercede for him.

As for subḥān Allāh: in Muslim's narration, “Subḥān Allāh and al-ḥamdu lillāh fills — or: fill — what is between heaven and earth,” the narrator was unsure what it is that fills what is between heaven and earth: the two phrases, or one of them?

In the narration of al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah: “Tasbīḥ and takbīr are the fill of heaven and earth,” and this narration is the more likely. Whether it means that both together fill what is between heaven and earth, or that each of them fills it, is open to either reading.
In the hadith of Abū Hurayrah and that of the other man, takbīr alone fills what is between heaven and earth.

In any case, tasbīḥ is below taḥmīd [saying al-ḥamdu lillāh] in merit, as is stated explicitly in the hadiths of ʿAlī, Abū Hurayrah, ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr and the man of Banū Sulaym: that tasbīḥ is half the Scale and al-ḥamdu lillāh fills it. The reason is that taḥmīd affirms all praises for Allah,

and so includes affirming all the attributes of perfection and all the qualities of majesty, whereas tasbīḥ is declaring Allah free of deficiencies, faults and defects; and affirmation is more complete than negation.

That is why tasbīḥ is never mentioned on its own, but always joined to something that indicates the affirmation of perfection. Sometimes it is joined to praise, as in saying subḥān Allāh wa-bi-ḥamdihi, and subḥān Allāh wa-l-ḥamdu lillāh;
and sometimes to one of the names that indicate greatness and majesty, as in His saying subḥān Allāh al-ʿAẓīm.
If the hadith of Abū Mālik shows that what fills what is between heaven and earth is tasbīḥ and takbīr together, the matter is plain. If it means that each of them fills that,
then the Scale is wider than what is between heaven and earth, so what fills the Scale is greater than what fills what is between heaven and earth.

This is shown by what is authentically reported from Salmān (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Scale will be set up on the Day of Resurrection, and if the heavens and the earth were weighed in it, it would hold them. The angels will say: Lord, for whom will You weigh with this?
Allah the Exalted will say: For whomever I will of My creation. The angels will say: Glory be to You! We have not worshipped You as You deserve to be worshipped.
Al-Ḥākim recorded it as marfūʿ and declared it authentic, but the mawqūf version, which stops short of the Prophet ﷺ, is the well-known one.

As for takbīr: in the hadiths of Abū Hurayrah and the man of Banū Sulaym, it alone fills what is between the heavens and the earth; and in the hadith of ʿAlī, takbīr together with tahlīl [saying lā ilāha illā Allāh] fills the heavens and the earth and what is between them.
As for tahlīl on its own, it reaches Allah with no veil between it and Him.
Al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said:
“No servant ever says lā ilāha illā Allāh sincerely but the gates of heaven are opened for it, until it reaches the Throne — so long as the major sins are avoided.”

Abū Umāmah said: There is no servant who utters a tahlīl that anything short of the Throne can hold back. It has also come, in the well-known hadith of the card (al-biṭāqah), that nothing equals it in the Scale.
Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasāʾī recorded it, and at its end, in Imam Aḥmad's version: “And nothing outweighs ‘In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful’.”
In the Musnad, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, the Prophet ﷺ said: “When death came to Nūḥ (peace be upon him), he said to his son:

I command you to say lā ilāha illā Allāh; for if the seven heavens and the seven earths were placed in one pan of the scale, and lā ilāha illā Allāh in the other, lā ilāha illā Allāh would outweigh them.”

It also has, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Mūsā (peace be upon him) said: Lord, teach me something by which I may remember You and call on You. He said: Mūsā, say lā ilāha illā Allāh.

He said: All Your servants say this; I want only something You single me out with. He said: Mūsā, if the seven heavens and those who inhabit them other than Me, and the seven earths, were in one pan, and lā ilāha illā Allāh in the other, lā ilāha illā Allāh would tip the scale against them.”
There is disagreement as to which of the two phrases is better:
the phrase of praise or the phrase of tahlīl?
Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr and others have related this disagreement.
Al-Nakhaʿī said: They used to hold that praise is the speech whose reward is most multiplied. Al-Thawrī said: No speech is multiplied like al-ḥamdu lillāh.
Praise includes affirming every kind of perfection for Allah, and so tawḥīd is included in it.

In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, from Abū Saʿīd and Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah has chosen four from among speech: subḥān Allāh, al-ḥamdu lillāh, lā ilāha illā Allāh and Allāhu akbar. Whoever says subḥān Allāh
has twenty good deeds written for him, or twenty bad deeds removed from him; whoever says Allāhu akbar, the same; whoever says lā ilāha illā Allāh, the same;
and whoever says al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn of his own accord has thirty good deeds written for him, or thirty bad deeds removed from him.”
This has also been narrated from Kaʿb as his own words, and it has been said that this is more authentic than the marfūʿ version.
His words ﷺ, “Prayer is light, charity is a proof, and patience is radiance” — in some copies of Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, “and fasting is radiance”:

these three kinds of deeds are all lights, but some of them are particular to one kind of light. Prayer is light without qualification. It is narrated, by two chains that are open to question, from Anas,
that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Prayer is the believer's light.” For believers in this world it is a light in their hearts and their inner sight, by which their hearts shine

and their inner sight is illumined. That is why it was the delight of the eyes of the God-fearing, as the Prophet ﷺ used to say: “The delight of my eye has been placed in prayer.” Aḥmad and al-Nasāʾī recorded it.
In one narration: “The hungry man is filled and the thirsty man's thirst is quenched, but I am never sated with love of prayer.”
In the Musnad, from Ibn ʿAbbās: Jibrīl said to the Prophet ﷺ: Allah has made prayer beloved to you, so take of it as much as you wish.
Abū Dāwūd recorded, from the hadith of a man of Khuzāʿah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Bilāl, call the iqāmah for the prayer and give us rest by it.”

Mālik ibn Dīnār said: I read in the Torah: Son of Ādam, do not fail to stand before Me in your prayer weeping, for I am the One who has drawn near to your heart, and in the unseen you have seen My light — meaning the tenderness and weeping that are opened to the one who prays, in his prayer.
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, from the hadith of ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, as marfūʿ: “When the servant guards his prayer, performing its wuḍūʾ, its bowing, its prostrations and its recitation properly,
it says to him: May Allah guard you as you have guarded me. And it is taken up to heaven, having a light, until it reaches Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and intercedes for the one who prayed it.”
It is a light for believers in their graves, especially the night prayer, as Abū al-Dardāʾ said: “Pray two rakʿahs in the darkness of the night for the darkness of the graves.”
Rābiʿah had for a time grown slack in her night devotions, and someone came to her in a dream and recited to her:
Your prayer is a light while people sleep, / and your sleep is a stubborn foe of prayer.
In the Hereafter it is a light for believers in the darknesses of the Resurrection and on the Bridge, for lights will be apportioned to them according to their deeds.
In the Musnad and the Ṣaḥīḥ of Ibn Ḥibbān, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, the Prophet ﷺ mentioned prayer
and said: “Whoever guards it, it will be a light, a proof and a salvation for him on the Day of Resurrection; and whoever does not guard it will have no light, no salvation and no proof.”
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, with a chain open to question, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said:

“Whoever prays the five prayers in congregation will cross the Bridge like flashing lightning in the first band of the foremost, and will come on the Day of Resurrection with his face like the moon on the night it is full.”

As for charity, it is a proof (burhān). The burhān is the ray that adjoins the face of the sun — hence the hadith of Abū Mūsā that the believer's soul leaves his body with a burhān like the burhān of the sun. Hence, too, a decisive argument is called a burhān,

because of how clearly it points to what it proves. In the same way, charity is a proof of the soundness of faith, and giving it willingly is a sign that the sweetness and taste of faith are present, as in the hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn Muʿāwiyah al-Ghāḍirī from the Prophet ﷺ:

“There are three things: whoever does them has tasted the taste of faith. Whoever worships Allah alone, [believing] that there is no god but Allah, and pays the zakāh on his wealth willingly, his soul urging him to it every year” — and he mentioned the hadith. Abū Dāwūd recorded it.
We mentioned a little earlier the hadith of Abū al-Dardāʾ about whoever pays the zakāh on his wealth willingly, in which the narrator said: And he used to say: None does that but a believer.

The reason for this is that souls love wealth and are miserly with it; so when a soul gives it freely for the sake of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that shows the soundness of its faith in Allah, His promise and His threat.
That is why the Arabs withheld the zakāh after the Prophet ﷺ, and al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him) fought them for withholding it. Prayer, too, is a proof of the soundness of one's Islam.
Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of Kaʿb ibn ʿUjrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Prayer is a proof.”

We mentioned in the commentary on the hadith “I have been commanded to fight people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, establish the prayer and pay the zakāh” that prayer is what distinguishes disbelief from Islam.

It is also the first thing a person will be called to account for on the Day of Resurrection: if his prayer is complete, he has succeeded and prospered. The hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr has already been cited, that for whoever guards it, it will be a light, a proof and a salvation on the Day of Resurrection.
As for patience, it is radiance (ḍiyāʾ). Radiance is light that carries a kind of heat and burning, like the radiance of the sun — unlike the moon, which is pure light,
shining without burning. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light” [Yūnus 10:5]. Hence Allah described the law of Mūsā as radiance,

as He said: “And We gave Mūsā and Hārūn the Criterion, and a radiance and a reminder for the God-fearing” [al-Anbiyāʾ 21:48] — though He also mentioned that the Torah contains light, as He said: “Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which was guidance and light” [al-Māʾidah 5:44]. But what predominates in their law is radiance, because of the burdens, shackles and heavy loads it contains.
And He described the law of Muḥammad ﷺ as light, because of the easy, upright religion (al-ḥanīfiyyah al-samḥah) it contains. The Exalted said:
“There has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book” [al-Māʾidah 5:15]. And He said:

“Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel, who commands them to do what is right and forbids them what is wrong, makes lawful for them the good things and forbids them the foul, and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them — those who believe in him, honour him, support him and follow the light sent down with him: it is they who will succeed” [al-Aʿrāf 7:157].

Since patience is hard on the soul, requiring one to struggle against the soul, restrain it and hold it back from what it craves, it is radiance. For the meaning of ṣabr in the language is confinement; hence qatl al-ṣabr, which is for a man to be held captive until he is killed.

Praiseworthy patience is of several kinds: patience in obeying Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; patience in refraining from disobeying Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; and patience with the decrees of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Patience in acts of obedience and in refraining from what is forbidden is better than patience with painful decrees. The Salaf stated this explicitly, among them Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Maymūn ibn Mihrān and others.
It has been narrated with a weak chain, from the hadith of ʿAlī as marfūʿ: “Patience under calamity earns the servant three hundred degrees;
patience in obedience earns him six hundred degrees; and patience in refraining from sins earns him nine hundred degrees.” Ibn Abī al-Dunyā and Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī recorded it.
One of the best kinds of patience is fasting, for it combines patience of all three kinds:
it is patience in obeying Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and patience in refraining from disobeying Allah,

because the servant leaves his desires for the sake of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, while his soul may be pulling him towards them. That is why the authentic hadith says: “Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: Every deed of the son of Ādam is for him except fasting; it is for Me, and I shall reward it.

He left his desire, his food and his drink for My sake.” It also involves patience with painful decrees, in the hunger and thirst the fasting person may suffer. The Prophet ﷺ used to call the month of fasting the month of patience.

In the hadith of the man of Banū Sulaym, the Prophet ﷺ said that fasting is half of patience. The secret of its being half of patience may well be harder to discover than the secret of purification's being half of faith. And Allah knows best.

His words ﷺ, “The Qurʾān is a proof for you or against you”: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “And We send down of the Qurʾān that which is healing and mercy for the believers, and it increases the wrongdoers only in loss” [al-Isrāʾ 17:82].
One of the Salaf said: No one ever sits with the Qurʾān and gets up from it just as he was;
rather, he either gains or loses. Then he recited this verse.

ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb narrated, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The Qurʾān will be given the form of a man on the Day of Resurrection. A man who bore it but went against its command will be brought,

and it will appear to him as an adversary and say: Lord, You made him bear me, and he was the worst of bearers: he overstepped my limits, neglected my obligations, committed disobedience to me and abandoned obedience to me. It will keep hurling arguments against him until it is said: He is yours to deal with. Then it will take him by the hand

and not let him go until it has thrown him face down into the Fire. And a righteous man who bore it and kept its command will be brought, and it will appear as an adversary on his behalf and say: Lord, You made him bear me, and he was the best of bearers: he kept my limits,

acted on my obligations, avoided disobedience to me and followed obedience to me. It will keep hurling arguments for him until it is said: He is yours to deal with. Then it will take him by the hand and not let him go until it has clothed him in a robe of brocade, set the crown of kingship on him and given him the cup of wine to drink.”

Ibn Masʿūd said: “The Qurʾān is an intercessor whose intercession is accepted, and an accuser whose word is believed. Whoever puts it before him, it leads him to Paradise; and whoever puts it behind his back, it leads him to the Fire.”

It is also related from him: “The Qurʾān will come on the Day of Resurrection and intercede for its companion, and be his guide to Paradise; or it will testify against him, and be his driver to the Fire.”

Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī said: This Qurʾān will be a reward for you or a burden on you. So follow the Qurʾān, and do not let the Qurʾān follow you; for whoever follows the Qurʾān, it brings him down into the meadows of Paradise, and whoever the Qurʾān follows, it pushes him from behind and hurls him into the Fire.

His words ﷺ, “Everyone goes out in the morning and sells himself, either freeing himself or ruining himself”: Imam Aḥmad and Ibn Ḥibbān recorded, from the hadith of Kaʿb ibn ʿUjrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “People go out in the morning in two kinds: one buys his soul — one freeing his soul, the other ruining it.”
In a narration recorded by al-Ṭabarānī: “People go out in the morning in two kinds: one sells his soul and ruins it, and one ransoms his soul and frees it.”

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “By the soul and Him who proportioned it, and inspired it with its wickedness and its taqwā: he has succeeded who purifies it, and he has failed who buries it” [al-Shams 91:7–10]. The meaning is:

he has succeeded who purifies his soul by obeying Allah, and he has failed who buries it in sins. Obedience purifies and cleanses the soul, so that it rises; while sins bury the soul and suppress it, so that it sinks low and becomes like something buried in the dust.
The hadith shows that every person is striving either for his soul's destruction or for its release. Whoever strives in obeying Allah has sold his soul to Allah

and freed it from His punishment; and whoever strives in disobeying Allah has sold his soul for disgrace and ruined it with sins that bring down Allah's anger and punishment. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said:

“Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their souls and their wealth in exchange for Paradise being theirs,” up to His words: “So rejoice in the bargain you have made with Him; that is the great success” [al-Tawbah 9:111]. The Exalted said:

“And among people is he who sells himself, seeking the pleasure of Allah; and Allah is Kind to His servants” [al-Baqarah 2:207]. And the Exalted said: “Say: The losers are those who will lose themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection; that is the clear loss” [al-Zumar 39:15].

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah: When “And warn your nearest kinsfolk” [al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:214] was revealed to him, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “People of Quraysh, buy yourselves from Allah; I cannot avail you anything against Allah. Banū ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib,
I cannot avail you anything against Allah.” In a narration of al-Bukhārī's: “Banū ʿAbd Manāf, buy yourselves from Allah. Banū ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib,
buy yourselves from Allah. Aunt of the Messenger of Allah, and Fāṭimah daughter of Muḥammad, buy yourselves, both of you, from Allah; I have no power to help you at all against Allah.”

In a narration of Muslim's, he called Quraysh, and when they had gathered he addressed them in general and in particular, saying: “Banū Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy, save yourselves from the Fire. Banū Murrah ibn Kaʿb, save yourselves from the Fire. Banū ʿAbd Shams, save yourselves from the Fire.

Banū ʿAbd Manāf, save yourselves from the Fire. Banū Hāshim, save yourselves from the Fire. Banū ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, save yourselves from the Fire. Fāṭimah, save yourself from the Fire. For I have no power to help you at all against Allah.”

Al-Ṭabarānī and al-Kharāʾiṭī recorded, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, as marfūʿ: “Whoever says in the morning subḥān Allāh wa-bi-ḥamdihi a thousand times has bought his soul from Allah the Exalted, and by the end of his day is freed from the Fire.”

A number of the Salaf bought their souls from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, with their wealth. Some gave their wealth away in charity, like Ḥabīb Abū Muḥammad; others gave in charity their own weight in silver three or four times, like Khālid al-Ṭaḥḥān.

Some would exert themselves in righteous deeds, saying: I am only a captive striving to free my neck — among them ʿAmr ibn ʿUtbah. One of them used to say twelve thousand tasbīḥs every day, the amount of his blood-money, as though he had killed himself and was ransoming himself with its blood-money.
Al-Ḥasan said: The believer in this world is like a captive striving to free his neck; he feels safe from nothing until he meets Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
He also said: Son of Ādam, you go out morning and evening in search of profits; so let your concern be your own soul, for you will never make a profit like it.

Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh said: A man once said to me when I was young: Free your neck as far as you can, while in this world, from the slavery of the Hereafter, for the captive of the Hereafter is never set free. He said: By Allah, I have never forgotten it since.
One of the Salaf used to weep and say: I do not have two souls; I have only one soul, and if it is lost I will not find another.
Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah said: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has made Paradise the price of your souls, so do not sell them for anything else.
He also said: Whoever holds his soul dear has no regard for this world.
He was asked: Who is the greatest of people in worth?
He said: The one who does not consider the whole world a worthy price for his soul.
One of the early poets recited:
I bargain my precious soul with its Lord, / for in all creation there is no price for it.
With it the Hereafter is gained; if I sell it / for anything of this world, that is the true loss.
If my soul is spent on some worldly gain I win, / then my soul is gone, and the price is gone too.
